title: How do group cases and written cases work, and how do you do well in them?
description: What to expect from group case exercises and written case interviews, used by the Big Four, Bain, Oliver Wyman and others, and how to stand out.
hook: In a group case, several candidates solve a business problem together while assessors watch, so you do well by improving the group's thinking without dominating it. In a written case, you work alone through a pack of data against the clock and then present, so you do well by finding the few exhibits that matter and leading with your answer. Both reward specific, practisable skills.
body:
In this guide

  • Who uses group and written cases
  • How group cases work
  • A worked group case: choosing a store site
  • How written cases work
  • A time plan for a 45-minute written case
  • Common mistakes
  • Practise now
  • Where to practise next

Who uses group and written cases

Most firms rely on one-to-one live cases, but these formats appear often enough to prepare for. A few examples, as of 2026:

  • Deloitte in Australia describes a student assessment day that can include a group case study and a one-to-one interview.
  • KPMG UK ends its graduate process with a half-day event of assessed activities; candidates report a group exercise and an analysis task.
  • Oliver Wyman and L.E.K. are reported to use written cases in later rounds in some offices.
  • Bain says some roles include a take-home written assignment, usually with about three days to complete it, which some candidates then present.

Formats change by office and year. Your invitation will tell you what to expect; if it does not, ask the recruiter. Firm-specific detail is in our guides to Deloitte, KPMG and Oliver Wyman.

How group cases work

Typically four to six candidates receive a business problem and some data, discuss it for a set time while assessors watch, and then present a recommendation. You are not competing to be the loudest. Assessors watch how you work with others as much as the quality of your ideas.

What good looks like

  • Suggest a structure early. "Shall we agree what the client is deciding, then split the data?"
  • Manage time. "Shall we agree how to split the time first, so we leave ten minutes to prepare the recommendation?"
  • Build on others. "Building on Amir's point about rent, that changes the ranking."
  • Bring quieter people in. "Lena, you were looking at the competitor data. What did you find?"
  • Summarise. Every ten minutes or so, play back where the group has got to.

What gets you marked down

  • Talking over people or repeating your point louder.
  • Going silent for long stretches.
  • Arguing for your favourite option before the group has agreed how to judge options.
  • Letting the group run out of time without a recommendation.

Good collaboration shows up in your questions and summaries, not in your airtime.

A worked group case: choosing a store site

Prompt: five candidates must recommend where a grocery chain should open its next store. There are three sites. Figures are illustrative.

SiteYearly contribution before rentYearly rentFit-out cost
A$1.2M$600k$1.5M
B$900k$250k$2.0M
C$1.0M$400k$1.2M

Step 1: agree the criteria before arguing

The most useful thing you can do early is propose an evaluation table: yearly profit after rent, investment, payback, customer access, strategic fit and main risk. Then split the work: one person on the numbers, one on location factors, one checking assumptions, one keeping time.

Step 2: run the numbers

  • Yearly profit after rent: A: $1.2M − $600k = $600k. B: $900k − $250k = $650k. C: $1.0M − $400k = $600k.
  • Payback: A: $1.5M ÷ $600k = 2.5 years. B: $2.0M ÷ $650k ≈ 3.1 years. C: $1.2M ÷ $600k = 2.0 years.
  • Five-year net, before discounting: A: 5 × $600k − $1.5M = $1.5M. B: 5 × $650k − $2.0M = $1.25M. C: 5 × $600k − $1.2M = $1.8M.

Step 3: find the insight

Site A has the strongest sales, but high rent wipes out the advantage. Site B makes the most each year, but its fit-out is so expensive that it comes last over five years. Site C, which nobody's instinct favoured, pays back fastest and leads over five years. That is the moment to say it to the group:

"Interesting: B wins on yearly profit, but C pays back in two years and is ahead of both A and B over five years. Unless B's location gives us something strategic, C looks strongest. Can we check the risks on C before we commit?"

That single contribution shows maths, judgement and collaboration. The group still needs to check market growth, competition and how easy each site is to operate before deciding. Our payback and NPV guide shows how to add discounting if the group has time.

How written cases work

You receive a pack of slides or data, work alone for a set time, then present, sometimes on slides you create and sometimes from notes. The trap is reading every page in detail. Some exhibits are there to test whether you can ignore them.

  1. Skim first. Find the question and the client's goal before reading any detail.
  2. Pick the exhibits that matter. Usually three or four answer the question.
  3. Do the key calculations and check them, writing units next to every number.
  4. Build a short story: answer first, two or three supporting points, risks, next steps. The pyramid principle is exactly this structure.
  5. Rehearse your opening sentence. It frames everything after it.

A time plan for a 45-minute written case

  • 5 minutes: read the question and skim every page without detail.
  • 15 minutes: pick the three or four exhibits that matter and do the calculations.
  • 15 minutes: write three or four slides or note pages: recommendation, two supporting points, risks and next steps.
  • 10 minutes: check numbers and rehearse your first two sentences.

If the time is shorter, keep the proportions. In the presentation, expect challenge. Defend your logic, accept a fair point gracefully, and say what extra data would change your mind.

Common mistakes

  • Group case: arguing for a favourite option before criteria are agreed. Propose the table first.
  • Group case: treating other candidates as rivals. Making others look bad rarely makes you look good.
  • Written case: running out of time on detail and presenting no clear answer.
  • Written case: slides with titles like "Market overview". Use headlines that state the finding: "Site C pays back in two years, fastest of the three."

Practise now

1. A fourth site, D, appears: contribution before rent $1.4M, rent $700k, fit-out $2.1M. Does it beat C?

Show the answer

Profit after rent: $1.4M − $700k = $700k a year, the highest of all. Payback: $2.1M ÷ $700k = 3 years. Five-year net: 5 × $700k − $2.1M = $1.4M. It beats C on yearly profit but loses on payback (3 years versus 2) and on five-year net ($1.4M versus $1.8M). C still leads unless the horizon is long: D's extra $100k a year takes nine years to make up its $900k higher fit-out cost.

2. Twenty minutes into a 30-minute group case, the group is still debating which site has the best footfall. What do you say?

Show the answer

"Good points on footfall. We have ten minutes left, so shall we park that as a risk, agree the recommendation on the numbers we have, and spend the last five minutes on who presents what?" You have kept time, respected the discussion and pushed the group to an answer.

3. Write a slide headline for this finding: online sales grew 30% while store sales fell 5%, and online is now a quarter of revenue.

Show the answer

"Online now drives a quarter of revenue and all of the growth, while stores decline." The headline states the so-what, so the reader knows the point before looking at the chart.

Where to practise next

Run a group case with three or four friends using a case from the PrepForCase casebook, rotating who keeps time and who summarises. For written cases, take a casebook case, give yourself 45 minutes alone with the data, and present to a friend. Our guide to practising with a partner shows how to give each other useful feedback.
